**Subtask 1: Greedy INA Switch Selection Based on Load-Capacity Proxy Scoring and Bottleneck Proximity**  
This subtask focuses exclusively on the initial placement of in-network aggregation (INA) switches under the strict budget constraint $K$, aiming to select a set of $K$ switches from the candidate pool $\text{ina\_candidates}$ that maximally reduce the overall iteration makespan by balancing traffic offloading with the risk of creating network hotspots. The core objective is to identify switches that can efficiently absorb large volumes of gradient traffic from multiple workers across concurrent jobs while remaining within their INA processing capacity $C_s$ and avoiding downstream link congestion toward the respective parameter servers (PS). To achieve this, a composite proxy score is computed for each candidate switch $s \in \text{ina\_candidates}$, defined as the ratio of the total expected incoming gradient rate (summed across all jobs and workers connected to switches in the same subtree as $s$) that would be routed to $s$ if INA were enabled, normalized by $C_s$, and adjusted by a congestion penalty factor. The expected incoming rate is estimated as $\sum_{j \in J} \sum_{w \in W_j} \gamma_{jw} \cdot \mathbb{I}_{\text{path}(w \to s) \text{ exists}}$, where $\gamma_{jw}$ is the gradient sending rate of worker $w$ in job $j$, and $\mathbb{I}$ is an indicator for path existence using the precomputed `network.allPathDict`. The congestion penalty is derived from the maximum link utilization (i.e., the ratio of load to capacity) along the path from $s$ to its associated PS $d_j$, computed as $\max_{e \in \text{path}(s \to d_j)} \left( \frac{l_e^{\text{s} \to \text{PS}}}{C_e^{\text{bw}}} \right)$, where $l_e^{\text{s} \to \text{PS}}$ is approximated using a baseline load model assuming uniform rate distribution. The final score is then:  
$$
\text{Score}(s) = \frac{\sum_{j} \sum_{w \in W_j} \gamma_{jw} \cdot \mathbb{I}_{\text{path}(w \to s) \text{ exists}}}{C_s \cdot \left(1 + \eta \cdot \max_{e \in \text{path}(s \to d_j)} \frac{l_e^{\text{s} \to \text{PS}}}{C_e^{\text{bw}}} \right)},
$$  
where $\eta > 0$ is a tunable weight (e.g., 1.0) emphasizing the importance of avoiding bottleneck links. Higher scores indicate switches that can handle more traffic relative to their capacity and are located on less congested paths. The algorithm sorts all candidate switches in descending order of this score and selects the top $K$ switches to deploy INA, ensuring the budget constraint $\sum_{s} x_s = K$ is satisfied. This process operates entirely within the topology and rate information provided in the input, using only precomputed paths, worker-to-job mappings, gradient volumes, and switch capacities, without relying on any optimization or assignment results from later stages. The selected set of switches is returned as a binary indicator vector over `ina_candidates`, forming the foundation for the subsequent routing phase.
